primers.title: Bits you declared, and the two ways of gluing circuits together
primers.body_md:
`QuantumCircuit(2)` gives you two qubits and ZERO classical bits, so `measure` has nowhere to write and raises `CircuitError`. `QuantumCircuit(2, 2)` gives both, auto-naming the registers `q` and `c` (which is why `add_register(QuantumRegister(2, 'q'))` on such a circuit then fails on the duplicate name). Building from explicit `QuantumRegister(3, 'data')` / `ClassicalRegister(2, 'c')` objects and passing them to the constructor is purely organizational — it lets you say `data[0]` instead of counting indices — and buys nothing at execution or transpile time.

`measure(qubit, cbit)` takes the qubit first and the clbit second, accepts ints, `Bit`s, registers, or parallel lists, and the mapping is entirely yours: `measure(0, 1)` really does store qubit 0's result in `c[1]`. (The keyword is `cbit`, not `clbit`, and naming the arguments never rescues a circuit with no classical bits.) The convenience methods are not neutral: `measure_all()` ALWAYS appends a fresh `ClassicalRegister` named `meas` sized to the qubit count — even when the circuit already has classical bits, leaving you with two registers and space-separated counts keys — and it inserts a `barrier` BEFORE the measurements. `measure_active()` behaves the same way but only measures qubits that carry operations.

Composition splits into two families, and the exam lives on the difference. `compose` is FUNCTIONAL by default: it returns a new circuit and leaves the caller untouched, so `base.compose(add_on)` with the result discarded is a silent no-op — assign the result back or pass `inplace=True`. It accepts a narrower operand and a `qubits=` list that maps the operand's qubits onto the target's, positionally: `qc.compose(sub, qubits=[0, 2])` sends `sub`'s qubit 0 to 0 and its qubit 1 to 2, so `sub.cx(0, 1)` becomes a CX from qubit 0 to qubit 2. `front=True` prepends instead of appending. `append`, by contrast, mutates in place and hands back an `InstructionSet`. `tensor` widens: in `a.tensor(b)` the CALLER `a` occupies the higher-index qubits and `b` the lower ones, so an X in `a` against an identity in `b` prepares `|10⟩`.

The structural accessors are cheap points. `num_qubits` and `num_clbits` are what they say; `width()` returns their SUM (qubits + clbits), not the qubit count; `size()` counts every operation including measures and each control-flow block as one; `depth()` is the critical path and is generally smaller than `size()`.

And the convention that colours everything downstream: results are little-endian. Bitstrings print as c_(n−1) … c_0 with classical bit 0 on the RIGHT, so flipping only qubit 0 of a three-qubit register and measuring all of it yields `'001'`.

primers.title: Control flow is context managers now — `c_if` is gone
primers.body_md:
A dynamic circuit is one whose later quantum operations depend, in real time, on a mid-circuit measurement result. That is the whole discriminator: measuring an ancilla and applying a correction gate when it returns 1 (teleportation, syndrome handling) needs one; sweeping an angle over many jobs, post-selecting shots after the fact, or letting the transpiler cancel gates does not — those are classical work done outside the QPU.

In Qiskit 2.x every conditional is a context manager on the circuit, and its condition is a `(classical_resource, value)` TUPLE: `with qc.if_test((cr[0], 1)): qc.x(1)`. The resource may be a single `Clbit` OR a whole `ClassicalRegister` — register-valued conditions are legal, so never accept "conditions must name one bit". Two spellings that look right and are not: `if_test(cr[0], 1)` (two positional arguments instead of a tuple) and `if_test(cr[0] == 1)`, which raises `TypeError: 'bool' object is not subscriptable` because `Clbit.__eq__` returns an ordinary Python bool. For anything richer than equality with a literal, build a condition from `qiskit.circuit.classical.expr` — `expr.equal(cr, 3)` compares the whole register as an integer and lifts the bare `3` for you, no `expr.lift` required.

The rest of the family follows the same shape. An else branch comes from the manager's return value: `with qc.if_test((cr[0], 0)) as else_: …` then `with else_: …`. `with qc.for_loop(range(3)):` repeats its body; the `as i` binding is optional and only needed if the body uses the index, and the body may hold any number of gates. `with qc.switch(cr[0]) as case:` opens `with case(0):`-style branches plus a fallback `with case(case.DEFAULT):`, which may be declared last. Careful with switch semantics: a value with no matching `case` falls through to DEFAULT, so `c0 = 1` against branches `case(0)` and `case(DEFAULT)` runs the DEFAULT body.

Everything the old API offered is removed, not deprecated. `InstructionSet.c_if` raises `AttributeError` in 2.x; there is no `condition=` gate keyword and no `.condition` attribute to assign; and the tempting plain-Python `if cr[0] == 1:` is not an error at all — it evaluates to False at build time, so no gate is added and nothing warns you.

One structural fact for output-prediction questions: each control-flow construct is stored as a SINGLE composite instruction, so `count_ops()` on a conditional circuit shows `if_else: 1` (or `for_loop`, `switch_case`), never the gates inside the body.

primers.title: Parameters are symbols; binding is functional and alphabetical
primers.body_md:
A `Parameter('theta')` is a symbolic placeholder you can put anywhere a gate angle goes, including inside arithmetic: `qc.rx(2 * t, 0)` and `qc.rz(t + np.pi / 2, 0)` build `ParameterExpression`s that are evaluated at bind time, so binding `t = π` yields 2π and 3π/2. A `ParameterVector('x', 3)` is a convenience wrapper creating three distinct parameters named `x[0]`, `x[1]`, `x[2]`; it does not auto-grow (`x[3]` is an `IndexError`) and its elements are ordinary parameters, not aliases of one another.

The single highest-yield fact in this objective: `qc.parameters` is a `ParameterView` sorted ALPHABETICALLY by name, not by insertion order. Add `gamma`, then `alpha`, then `beta`, and you get `['alpha', 'beta', 'gamma']`. `ParameterVector` elements are the one refinement — they sort by vector name and then by numeric index, so `x[10]` follows `x[9]` rather than `x[1]`; two separately-created `Parameter('x10')` and `Parameter('x2')` sort as plain strings, `x10` first.

That ordering is what makes list binding treacherous. `assign_parameters([0.5, 1.5])` binds POSITIONALLY against that sorted view, so on a circuit whose `rx` uses `theta` and whose `rz` uses `phi`, the list gives `phi = 0.5` and `theta = 1.5` — the reverse of the order the gates were added. A list must also supply one value per parameter: a short list raises `ValueError`, and a `ParameterVector` never broadcasts one value across its elements. A DICT is the safe form: it binds exactly the parameters it names, so `{q: 1.0}` on a three-parameter circuit is a legal *partial* binding leaving two free. Dict keys may be `Parameter` objects or their name strings, but matching is by identity, so a *different* `Parameter('th')` object built elsewhere raises `CircuitError: Cannot bind parameters (th) not present in the circuit`. A whole vector can be bound in one entry: `{x: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]}`.

Binding is functional, exactly like `compose`: `assign_parameters` RETURNS a new circuit and leaves the original parameterized (`inplace=True` opts out). So the source circuit keeps its free parameters and the returned one has zero. The legacy `bind_parameters` method is gone in Qiskit 2.x — `AttributeError`, not a deprecation warning.

Two consequences worth carrying into the exam. First, reusing ONE `Parameter` object on several gates ties them together: `num_parameters` stays 1 and a single binding sets every gate that references it — the mechanism behind weight-sharing ansätze. Second, parameters survive transpilation. You can transpile a parameterized circuit once into an ISA circuit and bind values afterwards, as many times as you like; the bound circuit keeps its layout and needs no second transpile. That transpile-once/bind-many pattern is the standard way to run a variational sweep.

primers.title: Six stages, four levels, one ISA target
primers.body_md:
Hardware runs ISA circuits only. A circuit obeys a backend's Instruction Set Architecture when it uses ONLY instructions in that backend's `Target` (its basis gates, measure, reset, control flow) AND every two-qubit gate sits on a pair connected in the `CouplingMap`. Both conditions, every time: an `h` on a basis of `{cx, rz, sx, x}` fails the first, a `cx(0, 4)` on a line fails the second. `decompose()` is not a substitute — it rewrites `h` into `u`, which is outside the IBM basis, so a decomposed circuit is still not ISA.

The recommended path is `pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=…, backend=…)` followed by `pm.run(qc)`. `.run()` is the only call that executes it — there is no `pm.transpile`, no `pm(qc)`, no `QuantumCircuit.transpile`; and `pm.run([qc])` returns a LIST, not a circuit. Without a backend object you can pass the constraints directly as `basis_gates=` plus `coupling_map=` (or a `Target`); `basis_gates` alone translates but never routes, so the result is not ISA.

The preset pipeline is always the same six-tuple of stages, in order: **init** (unroll to one- and two-qubit gates), **layout** (map virtual qubits to physical ones), **routing** (insert SWAPs so every two-qubit gate lands on a connected pair), **translation** (rewrite gates into the basis), **optimization** (simplify), **scheduling** (timing; the slot exists even with no scheduling method and simply runs empty). `pm.stages` reports exactly those names. Routing — not layout — is what inserts SWAPs; layout only chooses which physical qubits to start on.

Four optimization levels exist, 0 through 3; anything else, including 4, raises `ValueError`. Level 0 does the bare minimum with a trivial layout, level 1 adds light optimization and a layout search, level 2 drops trivial layout entirely and adds commutative cancellation, level 3 resynthesizes two-qubit blocks via KAK and runs unitarity-breaking passes on measurements. All four aim at the SAME target constraints — they differ in effort, not in the circuit's validity — and a higher level is not guaranteed to give fewer two-qubit gates on any particular circuit. In Qiskit 2.5 `generate_preset_pass_manager` carries `optimization_level=2` as a signature DEFAULT (and `transpile()` resolves an unspecified level to the same 2), so the old "the default is 1" lore is Qiskit 1.x; note that the docs page still describes the argument as a required positional one.

How much the level matters is mostly a layout story. A single `cx(0, 4)` on a five-qubit line becomes 10 CX at level 0 (trivial layout `[0,1,2,3,4]`, then SWAPs across four hops) but 1 CX at level 1, which simply picks an adjacent pair — the win is the layout, not gate cancellation. Pin the mapping yourself with `initial_layout=[2, 3, 4]`, an ordered virtual→physical list (virtual 0 → physical 2, and so on), not a set of allowed qubits. And a circuit wider than the device — 4 virtual qubits on a 3-qubit backend — has no valid layout at all and fails in the layout stage.

facts.fact_md: `QuantumCircuit(2)` has 2 qubits and ZERO classical bits, so `measure([0,1],[0,1])` raises `CircuitError`; use `QuantumCircuit(2, 2)` or add a `ClassicalRegister`.

`measure_all()` always appends a FRESH register named `meas` (even when the circuit already has clbits), and the instruction order is `… barrier, measure, measure` — the barrier goes before the measurements.
`compose` is functional by default: `base.compose(add_on)` returns a new circuit and leaves `base` unchanged — assign the result back or pass `inplace=True`.
`qc.compose(sub, qubits=[0, 2])` maps `sub`'s qubit 0 → 0 and qubit 1 → 2, so `sub.cx(0, 1)` becomes a CX with control 0 and target 2.
In `a.tensor(b)` the CALLER `a` takes the higher-index qubits: an X in `a` and an identity in `b` prepares `|10⟩`.
`width()` is qubits + clbits (3 + 2 = 5), `size()` counts all operations including measures (5), and `depth()` is the critical path (4) — the three are different numbers.
`measure(qubit, cbit)` honours whatever mapping you give it: `measure(0, 1)` and `measure(1, 0)` on `|q0⟩ = |1⟩` produce the bitstring `10` (c1 c0).
Counts are little-endian — flipping only qubit 0 of a 3-qubit register and calling `measure_all()` yields `001` on every shot.

Several named `QuantumRegister`/`ClassicalRegister` objects can be combined into one circuit, and `qc.find_bit(qubit)` reports both the bit's circuit index and its register — registers are an addressing and organization device.
The conditional API is `with qc.if_test((cr[0], 1)):` — a single TUPLE argument. `if_test(cr[0], 1)` and `if_test(cr[0] == 1)` are both wrong, and gates in the block become an `if_else` operation.
`InstructionSet.c_if` was REMOVED in Qiskit 2.0 (`AttributeError`); there is no `condition=` keyword and no `.condition` attribute — the context manager is the only route.

`if_test` conditions may reference a whole `ClassicalRegister`, not just a single `Clbit`; control-flow blocks appear as ONE operation in `count_ops()` (`if_else`, `for_loop`, `switch_case`); a `for_loop` body may hold any number of gates.
The else branch comes from the manager's return value: `with qc.if_test((cr[0], 0)) as else_:` … `with else_:` …, and both branches run against the same measured bit.
`with qc.for_loop(range(3)):` needs no `as i` when the body ignores the index; the body executes 3 times (three X gates leave the qubit at `|1⟩`).
`with qc.switch(cr[0]) as case:` supports `with case(0):` branches plus `with case(case.DEFAULT):` — a value with no matching case falls through to DEFAULT, which may be declared last.
`expr.equal(cr, 3)` is a valid `if_test` condition: it compares the register as an integer and lifts the bare Python `3` automatically (no `expr.lift` needed).

A dynamic circuit measures qubits MID-execution and then performs classical logic inside the circuit based on those outcomes (classical feedforward); Qiskit supports exactly four such constructs — `if_test`, `switch`, `for_loop`, `while_loop` — each returning a context manager for a `with` statement.
`qc.parameters` is sorted ALPHABETICALLY by name, not by insertion order: adding `gamma`, `alpha`, `beta` gives `['alpha', 'beta', 'gamma']`.
A list passed to `assign_parameters` binds positionally against that sorted view: `[0.5, 1.5]` on a circuit with `rx(theta)` then `rz(phi)` gives `phi = 0.5` and `theta = 1.5`.
A list must supply one value per parameter — a short list raises `ValueError`; a dict is the way to bind a subset.
`assign_parameters` is functional by default: the original circuit keeps its free parameters and the RETURNED circuit has them bound.
Dict binding is partial: `{q: 1.0}` on a three-parameter circuit leaves `p` and `r` free (`num_parameters` = 2).
Reusing one `Parameter` object on two gates keeps `num_parameters` at 1 and binds BOTH gates at once — the weight-sharing mechanism behind tied ansätze.
`ParameterVector('x', 3)` creates parameters named `x[0]`, `x[1]`, `x[2]`; `{x: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]}` binds all three at once, and `x[3]` raises `IndexError` (no auto-growth).
Parameter EXPRESSIONS are evaluated at bind time: with `t = π`, `rx(2*t)` becomes 2π ≈ 6.283 and `rz(t + π/2)` becomes 3π/2 ≈ 4.712.
Parameters survive transpilation — transpile once, then bind: the ISA circuit still holds its parameter, binding drops it to zero, and the bound circuit keeps its layout (no second transpile).
`generate_preset_pass_manager` defaults to `optimization_level=2` in Qiskit 2.5 (a signature default, backend-independent) — level 1 was `transpile()`'s default back in 1.x.
A preset `StagedPassManager` always has the same six stages in order: `init, layout, routing, translation, optimization, scheduling`.
`mitigation` and `sampling` are NOT transpiler stages — `layout`, `routing`, `translation`, and `scheduling` are.
Valid optimization levels are 0, 1, 2, 3 only — `optimization_level=4` raises `ValueError`.
A pass manager runs with `pm.run(qc)`; `pm.transpile(qc)`, `pm(qc)` and `qc.transpile(pm)` do not exist.
ROUTING is the stage that injects SWAPs to satisfy the coupling map; the layout stage only selects which physical qubits to use. The two are computed together by default but are logically distinct.

ISA means basis gates AND coupling map: an `h`, a `ccx`, a non-adjacent `cx`, or a circuit wider than the device all fail — and `decompose()` yields `u`, which is outside the basis, so it never produces an ISA circuit.
Measured routing cost: one `cx(0, 4)` on a 5-qubit line gives 10 CX at level 0 (trivial layout `[0,1,2,3,4]`) versus 1 CX at level 1 (layout `[0,4,2,3,1]`) — the win is LAYOUT, not gate cancellation.
`initial_layout=[2, 3, 4]` is an ORDERED virtual→physical map (virtual 0 → physical 2, 1 → 3, 2 → 4), not a set of permitted qubits.
Without a backend object, pass `basis_gates=` AND `coupling_map=` to `generate_preset_pass_manager`; `basis_gates` alone translates but does not route, so the output is not ISA.
The translation stage rewrites every non-basis gate: after transpiling to a `{cx, rz, sx, x, id}` basis, neither `h` nor `t` survives.

Higher levels buy more optimization at the cost of longer compile times, but not always a better circuit — the docs' own example gives identical two-qubit gate counts at levels 1 and 2, and only level 3 (KAK resynthesis) improves on them.

Docs level table: 0 = no optimization with `TrivialLayout`, 1 = light (trivial/VF2 layout + 1Q optimization + `InverseCancellation`), 2 = medium (no trivial layout + `CommutativeCancellation`), 3 = level 2 plus KAK resynthesis of two-qubit blocks and unitarity-breaking passes.

Arithmetic on a `Parameter` builds a `ParameterExpression`, not another `Parameter`: `2 * th` is an expression for which `isinstance(expr, Parameter)` is False (the subclass relation runs the other way), while the circuit still reports the single free `Parameter` in `qc.parameters`. Binding keeps the symbolic type — cast with `float(...)` if you need a number.

Named passes and their stages, read off a level-2 preset: `VF2Layout` and `SabreLayout` in `layout`; `CheckMap`, `SabreSwap` and `VF2PostLayout` in `routing`; `BasisTranslator` in `translation` (it also appears in `init` and in the optimization stage's re-translation loop); `Optimize1qGatesDecomposition` in `optimization`; `ConsolidateBlocks` in `init`.

`optimization_level=0` schedules no optimization pass at all. Measured on `h(0); cx(0,1); cx(0,1); t(1); h(2); z(2); z(2); cx(1,2); cx(0,2)` with no coupling map or basis gates: level 0 returns all nine gates unchanged, level 2 returns five — BOTH repeated pairs (`cx`-`cx` and `z`-`z`) cancel together. Cancellation is all-or-nothing across gate widths: no level removes the single-qubit pair while keeping the two-qubit one, and none deduplicates a pair down to a single surviving copy.

`with qc.for_loop(range(3)):` stores the body ONCE — the circuit keeps a single `for_loop` instruction, and the drawer renders it as one boxed region labelled with the index set verbatim (`For-0 range(0, 3)`), spanning every wire the body touches. Everything indented under the context manager belongs to the body, a statement written after the block is drawn outside the box, and a loop over `range(2)` labels its box `range(0, 2)`.
